haiku-low.q1: Accepted events get 202 only after Kafka acknowledges; rejected events are listed with reasons in the response. The rest of the batch continues.
haiku-low.q2: Timeouts and 503 cause a resend of the same batch with the same event_ids. 429 and other 5xx responses: NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q3: The earliest copy (smallest received_at, batch_id, position). Copies within 8 days are dropped; a copy after claim expiry may add a second row.
haiku-low.q4: Tuesday: its partition is the UTC date of received_at, and the Tuesday replay covers it. The client timestamp is ignored.
haiku-low.q5: A key-value store keyed by event_id, holding state, first_received_at, kafka_offset, owner and claimed_at. Entries expire by TTL of 8 days.
haiku-low.q6: Live consumer writes nothing and commits no offsets; events are re-read from Kafka. The archive is unaffected. Lag and p99 alerts fire.
haiku-low.q7: Claims stay pending and offsets uncommitted. After about 10 minutes a takeover reruns the write, which is idempotent on event_id, then commits.
haiku-low.q8: Reads raw archive objects for D-8 through D only. Rebuilt rows go to a staging table or partition, then swap into events_clean partition D.
haiku-low.q9: It reads archive copies from D-8 through D, picks the smallest (received_at, batch_id, position), and keeps it only if received_at falls in D.
haiku-low.q10: Before the swap, events_clean is untouched. Abort and restart the replay from its gate. The swap is one operation, so no partial state.
haiku-low.q11: Closed days whose archive and eight lookback days remain within the 90-day window; not before 02:00 UTC D+1 plus timeout T.
haiku-low.q12: Not decided. Options are drop or keep with a flag; product must decide before enrichment ships. The archive keeps all events either way.

sonnet.q1: It rejects only the bad events (missing event_id or device_id, or over 32 KB), logs each with a reason, and continues the rest of the batch. It returns 202 only after the accepted envelopes are appended to Kafka events_raw with acks=all and the producer acknowledges, listing each rejected event with its reason in the 202. If Kafka is unavailable it returns 503.
sonnet.q2: Timeout or no response: the client resends the same batch with the same event_ids. A 503 is handled the same way (resend the same batch). The document does not mention 429 or 5xx other than 503, so for 429 and other 5xx: NOT STATED. Rejected events are never resent.
sonnet.q3: The first copy, as long as the second arrives within W (8 days): the claim makes the later copy a duplicate that is dropped. If the second copy arrives after the claim expired (beyond W), it gets a second row in its own day, breaking first-copy-wins. A replay keeps the copy with the earliest received_at across D-8..D (only if that is in D).
sonnet.q4: Tuesday. The partition and replay are decided by the UTC date of received_at (set by the collector), never the client timestamp. So it belongs to Tuesday's partition and Tuesday's replay.
sonnet.q5: In a key-value (KV) store, as a claim keyed by event_id. The value is {state: pending/committed, first_received_at, kafka_offset, owner, claimed_at}. Entries are removed by TTL expiry: W = 8 days from the first accepted copy, not refreshed by later copies.
sonnet.q6: The live consumer makes no claim, no write and no offset commit, so the event is read again from Kafka. The archive is unaffected (events are still accepted and archived). Lag and p99 alerts fire. Whether the collector keeps accepting events is not contradicted: collector writes to Kafka independently of KV.
sonnet.q7: The claims stay pending and offsets are not committed, so nothing is lost. After about 10 minutes a takeover re-reads from the claim's kafka_offset and re-runs the write, which is idempotent on event_id so it keeps one row per event (no double counting), then sets claims committed and commits offsets. (How the takeover finds stale claims is an open question.)
sonnet.q8: A replay reads only the raw archive in object storage (received_date D-8 through D), never events_raw, KV (except the live-write check) or live offsets. Rebuilt rows are written to a staging table or partition for the run, which dashboards never read, until the swap.
sonnet.q9: It reads the archive for D-8 through D and, for each event_id with a copy in D, picks the copy with the smallest (received_at, batch_id, position) across all those days. It keeps that winner only if its received_at is in D. So an event whose first copy was received on an earlier day is not kept in D.
sonnet.q10: events_clean is untouched, because the swap hasn't happened and staging is separate. The operator aborts and restarts the replay from its gate. (A failed live-write check that cannot read KV is handled the same way.)
sonnet.q11: A closed day D, once the time is at least 02:00 UTC on D+1 plus the collector write timeout T, and only while the archives for D-8 through D still exist within the 90-day retention. Expired days cannot be rebuilt. Replays of different days can run in any order.
sonnet.q12: Not decided. Whether to drop or keep with a flag is an open question for product. The rule would be applied identically in live micro-batch write and replay, versioned, with replay using the version in force when requested. The archive keeps every accepted event either way.
